caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 703 of 1970
lawyer:
Abdus Salam with Md. Shahidul Huque----------For the Appellant. 
Md. Muksudur Rahman---------For Respondent No. 2. 
Anwarul Huque Chowdhury-----------For Respondent Nos. 1 and 3.
parties:
Khalilur Rahman--------- Plaintiff-Appellant.
Vs.
Province of East Pakistan and others-------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen, J.—This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against a judgment of reversal in a suit for declaration that the order dated 10.12.68 of the Deputy Commissioner, Faridpur in Misc. Case No. XIII E 26/67-68 involving the suit land is illegal, null and void, inoperative, without jurisdiction and not binding on the plaintiff and for a permanent injunction restraining the defendant No. 2 and also restraining the defendants from interfering with the plaintiff's possession in respect of the suitland. 

 6. Mr. Salam, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff has taken us through the judgments of the courts below and has also placed some evidence which, according to him, was not correctly construed by the learned District Judge while reversing the decision of the Trial Courts. Mr. Salam has contended that the Judgment of the learned District Judge is not proper judgment of reversal. According to the learned Advocate, the genuineness of the amolnama of Ext. I and Dakhila Ext, 2 was not challenged by the contesting defendant either in pleadings or in evidence. On consideration of the materials on record, it transpires that the contesting defendant did not challenge the genuineness of Exts. 1 and 2 in the pleadings. The case of defendant No. 1 as disclosed in the written statement is that "the story of the plaintiff's taking settlement of the suitland from the recorded tenant Mr. Ramesh Chandra Ghosal in 1952 before his leaving for India by amolnama is nothing but myth". A suggestion was thrown to the plaintiff, P.W.1 that the signatures of Ramesh Chandra Ghosal in amolnama and dakhila are forged, P.W.1, the plaintiff stoutly denied the suggestion. No evidence was adduced in favour of the contesting defendant indicating that the Exts. 1 and 2 were not genuine and that the same did not bear the signature of Ramesh Chandra Ghosal, The Trial Court on consideration of the plaintiff's evidence as regards the execution of Exts. 1 and 2 clearly found that the plaintiff proved the story of lease. The learned District Judge, it appears, was of the view that Exts 1 and 2 appear to have been written in the same sitting by the same hands with the same pen and ink. Ext. 1 was besmeared with oil in order that it might look old". The learned District, Judge was also of the view that Vie dakhila Ext. 2 does not belong to the estate of Ramesh Chandra Ghosal. It appears to be a Dakhila book available in the marker". Being of the above view, the learned District Judge concluded "the Exts. 1 and 2 are manufactured papers for the purpose of this suit". The finding of the learned District Judge is not supported by the evidence on record. Mr. Salam has rightly pointed out that the finding of the learned District Judge that Exts. 1 and 2 are manufactured papers created for the purpose of this suit is based on surmises and conjectures which formed the basis of the aforesaid finding. Mr. Anawarul Hoque Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 could not point out from the record, the evidence on which the aforesaid findings of the learned District Judge could be maintained. He, however, contended that the question of genuineness and otherwise of Exts. 1 and 2 being a question of fact, the High Court, under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no jurisdiction to interfere. Suffice it to say, that a finding of fact not based on evidence but on mere surmises and conjectures is not a legal and valid finding of fact. Accordingly we are of opinion that such finding is open to interference is second appeal u/s 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 7. Mr. Salam next contends that the finding of possession recorded by the learned District Judge is not supported by the evidence on record, The learned Advocate has referred to the relevant evidence of the P.Ws. and also of D.W.I. indicating that the learned Subordinate Judge decided the question of possession upon a correct assessment and appreciation of the evidence. According to the learned Advocate the finding on possession by the learned District Judge is the result of wrong interpretation of evidence. On the one hand, the learned District Judge finds that it is difficult to come to the conclusion that the plaintiff has been in possession of the statutory period," on the other hand, be finds that the plaintiff "is a trespasser". On these materials, the learned District Judge was of the view that the Court cannot believe the plaintiff's continuous possession for a period of more than 12 years. My view is that under the circumstances the plaintiff cannot claim any interest in the suitland so that he may be in a position to resist the defendants". Mr. Salam points out that defendant No, 2 who claims to be in. possession of the suitland on the basis of his alleged settlement  from the defendant No. 2 did not contest the suit by filing a written statement. He did not depose in the suit asserting his possession in the suit land. D.W. 2 Akmoi Khan, the father-in-law of defendant No. 1 deposed in the suit claiming possession of the defendant No. 2, This witness is a process server attached to the office of S.D.O. Madaripur, No document showing delivery of possession in favour of the defendant No. 2 is forthcoming, There is also no evidence that the defendant No. 1 took over possession of the suitland from the plaintiff and was in possession thereof before granting the impugned settlement in favour of the defendant No 2. On the other hand the evidence of D.W. 1 clearly indicates that the possession was not taken back from the plaintiff and that he is still in possession. "It may be pointed out that this witness Ismail Dhali is a Tahshilder in the Enemy Property Department at Madaripur, He is the person who went to the suitland 1 or 1 months after the Gazette Notification by E. P. M. C. and he found the plaintiff in possession of the suitland. He also ascertained from the neighbours that the plaintiff was actually in possession from before. The learned Subordinate Judge took into consideration the evidence of the P. Ws. 1 and reached a clear finding that P. Ws. 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are disinterested witnesses and proved the plaintiff's possession apart from the evidence of D.W.I. In the circumstances, the learned District Judge does not appear to have directed his considerations on these vital aspects of the evidence of P. Ws. while doubting the plaintiff's possession and consequently disbelieving the plaintiff's continuous possession for over 12 pears. It is curious to note that the learned District Judge finds the plaintiff to be a trespasser which clearly indicates that the plaintiff is in possession. Mr. Salam has drawn our attention to the case of Naresh Chandra Nandi Vs. Deputy Commissioner Dacca and others, 28 D.L.R. 437. The learned Advocate submits that even according to the learned District Judge, the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land as a trespasser and it has not been proved that possession was taken away by the defendant No. 1 so as to acquire the lawful authority to grant settlement of the suitland in favour of defendant No 2. The contention is not without substance. Mr. A.H. Chowdhury found it difficult to support the learned District Judge in the view expressed by him on the question of possession. He, however, repeated his contention that the said finding is a finding of fact. We are of the opinion that the finding of fact, not supported by evidence and inconsistent on the face of it, cannot be regarded as a valid finding on a question of fact. It further appears that the learned District Judge took exception with regard to the plaintiff that since he was in Army he could not be in possession of the suitland for 20 years. The learned District Judge does not appear to have applied the same yard-stick in considering the question of the possession of defendant No. 2 who is also serving in Army. It is evident that the learned District Judge did not correctly approach and construe the evidence of the P.Ws. on the question of possession while holding that the evidence regarding possession given by. the P. Ws. cannot be reconciled with the evidence given by the plaintiff himself". The learned District Judge does not appear to have assigned any cogent reason in qualifying P. Ws. 4, 5, 6 and 7 as "procured witnesses" and P. W. 6 as a Criminal, P. Ws. 6 and 7 are the  attesting witnesses to Ext. 1, the amolnama. The evidence of P. W. 3 Tarakeshwer Chaterjee found inadequate consideration by the learned District Judge. It is true that the appellate Court is not bound by the finding of the Trial Court on a question fact but it must always be remembered that the appellate Court has not the same opportunity of appreciating the evidence which the trial Court has, in view of the fact that the witnesses deposed in the tatter's presence and the latter had the opportunity of studying their behaviour. There is always a balance in favour of the judgment of the trial Court. It is evident that the lower appellate Court reversed the judgment of the trial Court on material questions without considering the facts and circumstances upon which it stands. High Court in such circumstance will interfere with the judgment of the first appellate Court even if the question involved is a question of fact. It appears that the judgment of the trial Court is based on perception of facts and the learned District Judge, lightly brushed aside the findings of the trial Court which appear to be supported by evidence and cogent reasons behind them, In the circumstances, the contention of Mr. Salam that the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal is not with substance. 

 10. For the reasons stated above the contention of Mr. Salam that the judgment of Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal is of substance.
